source.title: Distance-Based Weight Transfer for Fine-Tuning From Near-Field to Far-Field Speaker Verification
source.authors: Li Zhang; Qing Wang; Hong-Ji Wang; Yue Li; Wei Rao; Yan-Nan Wang; Linfu Xie

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a weight-distance regularizer changes overfitting during fine-tuning, using speaker-verification performance and training/validation trends. It does not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates weight transfer regularization during near-field to far-field speaker-verification fine-tuning. Its weight-distance regularizer and speech-domain setting do not match a listed version; relevant findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates weight transfer regularization for speaker-verification fine-tuning and cites Jiang et al. on generalization theory. It tests none of V1–V8: distance from pre-trained weights is neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor dropout, and using Adam without an optimizer comparison does not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they claim WTR alleviates overfitting and catastrophic forgetting and derive a tighter PAC-Bayes bound. The reported experiments show improved far-field verification performance and qualitative overfitting trends; they do not separately measure retention on the original near-field task.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses distance-based weight transfer regularization for near-field to far-field speaker-verification fine-tuning; it does not test the listed claim-version recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The three WTR norms yield different EER/minDCF values; FFSVC 2020 and FFSVC 2022 results differ. L2-norm WTR has the lowest reported EER/minDCF on both datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: All three WTR variants reduce reported EER and minDCF relative to vanilla fine-tuning on both development-trial sets. L2 WTR reduces EER from 7.435% to 5.887% on FFSVC 2020 and from 8.041% to 6.702% on FFSVC 2022. Section 4.2 describes reduced training/validation divergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining distance from pre-trained weights can improve far-field speaker-verification performance and mitigate overfitting during fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing
record.problems: The epoch-wise trend results are described without numeric values in the text; uncertainty estimates are not stated. The reported setting is far-field speaker verification, not the natural-label image or language classification settings in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Natural-label versus fixed-random-label fitting and held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed to fit.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimization and the effects of tuning or optimizer changes.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects, training-set size, underfitting, and removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 values match the record. Section 3.1 identifies the evaluation trials as development trials, and Section 3.2 says models are evaluated on these sets to select the best models. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The PAC-Bayes argument concerns distance from pre-trained weights, not the perturbation-based sharpness measure in V7.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures on image datasets.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and their tuning.
Large versus small batch sizes and training-recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.value: Training loss decreases while EER increases; the authors state that generalization error keeps increasing.
rows.note: Trend is described in the text; numeric figure values are not provided.
rows.check: Section 4.2 describes decreasing training loss and increasing EER, interpreting this as overfitting. The measure should identify validation EER rather than imply increasing training EER. This trend tests no listed version.
